I was a sickly, delicate boy, suffered much from asthma, and frequently had to be taken away on trips to find a place where I could breathe. One of my memories is of my father walking up and down the room with me in his arms at night when I was a very small person, and of sitting up in bed gasping, with my mother and father trying to help me.

Christmas was an occasion of literally delirious joy. In the evening we hung up our stockings - or rather the biggest stockings we could borrow from the grown-ups -and before dawn we trooped in to open them while sitting on Father's and Mother's bed; and the bigger presents were arranged, those for each child on its own table in the drawing room, the doors to which were thrown open after breakfast.
Morning prayers were with my father. We used to stand at the foot of the stairs and when father came down we called out 'I speak for you and the cubby-hole, too!'

My father, Theodore Roosevelt, was the best man I ever knew. he combined strength and courage with gentleness, tenderness, and great unselfishness. He would not tolerate in us children selfishness or cruelty, idleness, cowardice, or untruthfulness.

We children, of course, loved the country beyond anything. We disliked the city. We were always wildly eager to get to the country when Spring came, and very sad when in the late Fall the family moved back to town.

text: Tried snowshoing for the first time. Went about six miles, making the round of Will Dow's "lucivee' [lynx] traps, which however contained nothing. The woods looked simply perfect, all the evergreens being loaded with snow; I have never seen a grander sight than these northern forests in winter. I got along very well, except in a cedar swamp. We saw many tracks of lucivees, foxes, otters and rabbits; and found a porcupine up in a hemlock. I brought him down quite neatly with the rifle.

original.title: Theodore Roosevelt Papers: Series 8: Personal Diaries, 1878-1884; Vol. 2, 1879, Jan. 1-Dec. 31

text: Read my bible in the morning. In the afternoon took a tramp through the woods; I can not get used to the extreme beauty of the snow covered pine and spruce forests. The cold does not bother me at all in the woods, but if there is any wind it is very disagreeable in the open. I get along very well on snow shoes, but the swamps are very tough work - although perhaps not so bad as in summer. There is very little life in the woods.

original.title: Theodore Roosevelt Papers: Series 8: Personal Diaries, 1878-1884; Vol. 2, 1879, Jan. 1-Dec. 31

text: Went off on a tramp through the woods with Will Dow. Walked up to Dyer Brook, then a couple of miles along it, and then struck out in the woods. The best walking was on the hard wood grounds; it was fearfully hard work in some of the thick, swampy spruce and cedar thickets, but not as bad as in summer. I saw an arctic woodpecker by a stream and some Halldronian chickadees in a spruce wood, and two whiskey jacks came round us at lunch time; we saw two or three hare tracks, and once the round footprints of a canada lynx, and found where a spruce partridge had passed the night; but in an 8 hour tramp, these were the only traces of life.

original.title: Theodore Roosevelt Papers: Series 8: Personal Diaries, 1878-1884; Vol. 2, 1879, Jan. 1-Dec. 31

text: Spent the day tramping through the woods with Will Seawall. We saw a good many tracks of lucivees, foxes, rabbits, otters, minks, weasels, squirrels, porcupines + c; but the only living creatures were a couple of chickadees and a woodpecker. Finally we found the footprints of a partridge on some hardwood ground, and following them up roused the bird from under a fallen birch top, and I shot it. The snow shoing [sic] is poor, the snow being wet or heavy, and the weather warmish. 1 ruffed grouse.

original.title: Theodore Roosevelt Papers: Series 8: Personal Diaries, 1878-1884; Vol. 4, 1881, Jan. 1-Dec. 26

original.title: Theodore Roosevelt Papers: Series 8: Personal Diaries, 1878-1884; Vol. 4, 1881, Jan. 1-Dec. 26

text: Hurrah! for a summer abroad with the darling little wife.

original.title: Theodore Roosevelt Papers: Series 8: Personal Diaries, 1878-1884; Vol. 4, 1881, Jan. 1-Dec. 26

original.title: Theodore Roosevelt Papers: Series 8: Personal Diaries, 1878-1884; Vol. 4, 1881, Jan. 1-Dec. 26

text: Alice gets worse.

original.title: Theodore Roosevelt Papers: Series 8: Personal Diaries, 1878-1884; Vol. 4, 1881, Jan. 1-Dec. 26

text: Alice is sicker than ever; I am still in beautiful health.

original.title: Theodore Roosevelt Papers: Series 8: Personal Diaries, 1878-1884; Vol. 4, 1881, Jan. 1-Dec. 26

text: Confound a European trip, say I! Alice wretchedly sick; I have'n't been at all sick but tired out by taking care of her.

original.title: Theodore Roosevelt Papers: Series 8: Personal Diaries, 1878-1884; Vol. 4, 1881, Jan. 1-Dec. 26

text: Landed at Queenstown. Alice revived at once, very much. Steamed up the River to Cork; most beautiful sail. At Imperial Hotel good.

original.title: Theodore Roosevelt Papers: Series 8: Personal Diaries, 1878-1884; Vol. 4, 1881, Jan. 1-Dec. 26

text: Flowers all out; birds singing; everything lovely.

original.title: Theodore Roosevelt Papers: Series 8: Personal Diaries, 1878-1884; Vol. 4, 1881, Jan. 1-Dec. 26

text: Boat home. Scenery lovely. Hurrah!

original.title: Theodore Roosevelt Papers: Series 8: Personal Diaries, 1878-1884; Vol. 4, 1881, Jan. 1-Dec. 26

text: We drove to Dunloe's Gap; Alice on pony, I walked through it; very wild and grand

original.title: Theodore Roosevelt Papers: Series 8: Personal Diaries, 1878-1884; Vol. 4, 1881, Jan. 1-Dec. 26

text: Poor devil fainting from hunger. Had him fed + sent to cork.

original.title: Theodore Roosevelt Papers: Series 8: Personal Diaries, 1878-1884; Vol. 4, 1881, Jan. 1-Dec. 26

text: Alice is best travelling companion I have ever known. By Jove, what luck I have had! This is the lovliest trip I ever was on.

original.title: Theodore Roosevelt Papers: Series 8: Personal Diaries, 1878-1884; Vol. 4, 1881, Jan. 1-Dec. 26

text: Lovely scenery. Are leading most luxurious life.

original.title: Theodore Roosevelt Papers: Series 8: Personal Diaries, 1878-1884; Vol. 4, 1881, Jan. 1-Dec. 26

text: They are all too kind for anything.

original.title: Theodore Roosevelt Papers: Series 8: Personal Diaries, 1878-1884; Vol. 4, 1881, Jan. 1-Dec. 26

text: Spent the afternoon with Uncle Irvine + Aunt Ella; they have a most lovely little house.

original.title: Theodore Roosevelt Papers: Series 8: Personal Diaries, 1878-1884; Vol. 4, 1881, Jan. 1-Dec. 26

original.title: Theodore Roosevelt Papers: Series 8: Personal Diaries, 1878-1884; Vol. 4, 1881, Jan. 1-Dec. 26

original.title: Theodore Roosevelt Papers: Series 8: Personal Diaries, 1878-1884; Vol. 4, 1881, Jan. 1-Dec. 26

original.title: Theodore Roosevelt Papers: Series 8: Personal Diaries, 1878-1884; Vol. 4, 1881, Jan. 1-Dec. 26

original.title: Theodore Roosevelt Papers: Series 8: Personal Diaries, 1878-1884; Vol. 4, 1881, Jan. 1-Dec. 26

text: British museum (beautiful sculptures)

original.title: Theodore Roosevelt Papers: Series 8: Personal Diaries, 1878-1884; Vol. 4, 1881, Jan. 1-Dec. 26

original.title: Theodore Roosevelt Papers: Series 8: Personal Diaries, 1878-1884; Vol. 4, 1881, Jan. 1-Dec. 26

original.title: Theodore Roosevelt Papers: Series 8: Personal Diaries, 1878-1884; Vol. 4, 1881, Jan. 1-Dec. 26

original.title: Theodore Roosevelt Papers: Series 8: Personal Diaries, 1878-1884; Vol. 4, 1881, Jan. 1-Dec. 26

original.title: Theodore Roosevelt Papers: Series 8: Personal Diaries, 1878-1884; Vol. 4, 1881, Jan. 1-Dec. 26

original.title: Theodore Roosevelt Papers: Series 8: Personal Diaries, 1878-1884; Vol. 4, 1881, Jan. 1-Dec. 26

text: This summer I have passed travelling through Europe and though I have enjoyed it greatly, yet the more I see the better satisfied I am that I am an American; free born and free bred.
Capt. A. Thompson gave us a dinner and a box at the theatre.

original.title: Theodore Roosevelt Papers: Series 8: Personal Diaries, 1878-1884; Vol. 4, 1881, Jan. 1-Dec. 26

text: Went to see Colonel Sawler at the Tower.

original.title: Theodore Roosevelt Papers: Series 8: Personal Diaries, 1878-1884; Vol. 4, 1881, Jan. 1-Dec. 26

text: Came on to Liverpool to stay with Uncle Irvine.

original.title: Theodore Roosevelt Papers: Series 8: Personal Diaries, 1878-1884; Vol. 4, 1881, Jan. 1-Dec. 26

text: Have enjoyed the time so much. Spend most of the day with the dear old sea captain, Uncle Jimmie Bulloch.

original.title: Theodore Roosevelt Papers: Series 8: Personal Diaries, 1878-1884; Vol. 4, 1881, Jan. 1-Dec. 26

text: Bob Grant aboard very pleasant.

original.title: Theodore Roosevelt Papers: Series 8: Personal Diaries, 1878-1884; Vol. 4, 1881, Jan. 1-Dec. 26

text: Alicey really enjoys the voyage.

original.title: Theodore Roosevelt Papers: Series 8: Personal Diaries, 1878-1884; Vol. 4, 1881, Jan. 1-Dec. 26

text: Arrived. All of both families met us.

original.title: Theodore Roosevelt Papers: Series 8: Personal Diaries, 1878-1884; Vol. 4, 1881, Jan. 1-Dec. 26

text: Am going to try to kill our last years legislator.

original.title: Theodore Roosevelt Papers: Series 8: Personal Diaries, 1878-1884; Vol. 4, 1881, Jan. 1-Dec. 26

text: Out to Oyster Bay to pass Sunday.

original.title: Theodore Roosevelt Papers: Series 8: Personal Diaries, 1878-1884; Vol. 4, 1881, Jan. 1-Dec. 26

text: Alice is up in Boston. Am living entirely alone in the house, with old Dora to take care of me.

original.title: Theodore Roosevelt Papers: Series 8: Personal Diaries, 1878-1884; Vol. 4, 1881, Jan. 1-Dec. 26

text: Am working fairly hard at my law, hard at politics, and hardest of all at my book, ('Naval History.') which I expect to publish this winter.

original.title: Theodore Roosevelt Papers: Series 8: Personal Diaries, 1878-1884; Vol. 4, 1881, Jan. 1-Dec. 26

text: Much to my surprise was nominated to the Assembly from the 21st district. My platform is; strong Republican on State matters, but independent on local and municipal affairs.

original.title: Theodore Roosevelt Papers: Series 8: Personal Diaries, 1878-1884; Vol. 4, 1881, Jan. 1-Dec. 26

text: Uncle Jim, Em + Al bitterly opposed to any candidacey [sic] of course.

original.title: Theodore Roosevelt Papers: Series 8: Personal Diaries, 1878-1884; Vol. 4, 1881, Jan. 1-Dec. 26

text: Most of my friends are standing by me like trumps.

original.title: Theodore Roosevelt Papers: Series 8: Personal Diaries, 1878-1884; Vol. 4, 1881, Jan. 1-Dec. 26

text: Have a good chance of being elected if I am not sold out.

original.title: Theodore Roosevelt Papers: Series 8: Personal Diaries, 1878-1884; Vol. 4, 1881, Jan. 1-Dec. 26

text: Much to my surprise was nominated to the Assembly from

original.title: Theodore Roosevelt Papers: Series 8: Personal Diaries, 1878-1884; Vol. 4, 1881, Jan. 1-Dec. 26

text: All my friends stand by me like trumps, except Al, Em + Uncle Jim.

original.title: Theodore Roosevelt Papers: Series 8: Personal Diaries, 1878-1884; Vol. 4, 1881, Jan. 1-Dec. 26

text: owned by no man
untrammelled and unpledged
My platform is Republican, but Independent on Municipal matters.

original.title: Theodore Roosevelt Papers: Series 8: Personal Diaries, 1878-1884; Vol. 4, 1881, Jan. 1-Dec. 26

text: Was elected to the Legislature from the 21st Assembly District by a majority of 1501

original.title: Theodore Roosevelt Papers: Series 8: Personal Diaries, 1878-1884; Vol. 4, 1881, Jan. 1-Dec. 26

text: I have become a "political hack!"
All of the family are in town.

original.title: Theodore Roosevelt Papers: Series 8: Personal Diaries, 1878-1884; Vol. 4, 1881, Jan. 1-Dec. 26

text: News Boys lodging house as usual.

text: Book is in the hands of the publishers - Putnams.

original.title: Theodore Roosevelt Papers: Series 8: Personal Diaries, 1878-1884; Vol. 4, 1881, Jan. 1-Dec. 26

text: The going out has fairly begun; all are it, from dinners to Balls.

original.title: Theodore Roosevelt Papers: Series 8: Personal Diaries, 1878-1884; Vol. 4, 1881, Jan. 1-Dec. 26

text: Am trying to work up an Aqueduct Bill.

original.title: Theodore Roosevelt Papers: Series 8: Personal Diaries, 1878-1884; Vol. 4, 1881, Jan. 1-Dec. 26

text: I think we shall live with Mother another winter.

original.title: Theodore Roosevelt Papers: Series 8: Personal Diaries, 1878-1884; Vol. 4, 1881, Jan. 1-Dec. 26

text: Celebrated Xmas as usual.

original.title: Theodore Roosevelt Papers: Series 8: Personal Diaries, 1878-1884; Vol. 4, 1881, Jan. 1-Dec. 26

text: Alice is at Montreal with the girls on their great party; so I am keeping house with Mother, while wee Wifie is absent.

original.title: Theodore Roosevelt Papers: Series 8: Personal Diaries, 1878-1884; Vol. 5, 1882, Jan. 1-Feb. 15

text: Went up to Albany to begin my duties in the legislature. Attended the Republican Caucus, at which 'Old Salt' Alvord was nominated for speaker; I voted against him.

original.title: Theodore Roosevelt Papers: Series 8: Personal Diaries, 1878-1884; Vol. 5, 1882, Jan. 1-Feb. 15

text: The Assembly opened. We were all sworn in, and then adjourned.

original.title: Theodore Roosevelt Papers: Series 8: Personal Diaries, 1878-1884; Vol. 5, 1882, Jan. 1-Feb. 15

text: The legislature has assembled in full force; 128 assemblymen, . . . 61 Republicans, 8 Tammany among 67 Democrats - Tammany holds the 'balence of power'

Ballotted for speaker. There are 61 Republicans in the house; there are 67 democrats, but of these 7 are Tammany Hall men, who are 'striking' for their own candidate, and so a deadlock has come about, Adjourned till Monday.

original.title: Theodore Roosevelt Papers: Series 8: Personal Diaries, 1878-1884; Vol. 5, 1882, Jan. 1-Feb. 15

text: My book seems to be getting on rather slowly.

original.title: Theodore Roosevelt Papers: Series 8: Personal Diaries, 1878-1884; Vol. 5, 1882, Jan. 1-Feb. 15

text: Back to the legislature again.

original.title: Theodore Roosevelt Papers: Series 8: Personal Diaries, 1878-1884; Vol. 5, 1882, Jan. 1-Feb. 15

text: I very much like my fellow members as a whole, especially those from the country; the city members are of a much poorer stamp, especially the democrats, who are mainly Irishmen. The wrangling goes on with great bitterness between the Tammany and Anti tammany factions; while we Republicans can look on with indifference.

original.title: Theodore Roosevelt Papers: Series 8: Personal Diaries, 1878-1884; Vol. 5, 1882, Jan. 1-Feb. 15

text: They are a stupid, sodden vicious lot, most of them being equally deficient in brains and virtue.
I went on to Boston.

original.title: Theodore Roosevelt Papers: Series 8: Personal Diaries, 1878-1884; Vol. 5, 1882, Jan. 1-Feb. 15

text: Came back to Albany.

original.title: Theodore Roosevelt Papers: Series 8: Personal Diaries, 1878-1884; Vol. 5, 1882, Jan. 1-Feb. 15

text: By God, McManus, I understand you are going to toss me in a blanket. If you try anything like that, I'll kick you, I'll bite you, I'll do anything to you.
You'd better let me alone.
Attended the funeral of Senator Wagner.

original.title: Theodore Roosevelt Papers: Series 8: Personal Diaries, 1878-1884; Vol. 5, 1882, Jan. 1-Feb. 15

text: Adjourned and Alice and I went down to New York.

text: Returned to Albany.

text: Made my first speech (which was very well received) advising a policy of strict neutrality between the warring democratic factions.

original.title: Theodore Roosevelt Papers: Series 8: Personal Diaries, 1878-1884; Vol. 5, 1882, Jan. 1-Feb. 15

text: Mr. Spee-kar, Mr. Spee-kar
Adjourned; but as Alice and I are all settled here, with our books and everything, as comfortable as possible, we decided to spend Sunday here in Albany.

original.title: Theodore Roosevelt Papers: Series 8: Personal Diaries, 1878-1884; Vol. 5, 1882, Jan. 1-Feb. 15

text: Legislature reopenned. Deadlock still in force.

original.title: Theodore Roosevelt Papers: Series 8: Personal Diaries, 1878-1884; Vol. 5, 1882, Jan. 1-Feb. 15

text: Deadlock broken at last: the Tammnay [sic] men made some sort of bargain, and the Regular Democratic candidate for speaker was elected and installed.

text: Alice and I shall stay in Albany.

text: The Tilden and Tammany Democrats combined to elect speaker Patterson - (apparently a good man) but the deadlock seems to be as complete as ever as regards the rest of the slate.

text: Adjourned,- without doing anything - Alice and I went to New York.

original.title: Theodore Roosevelt Papers: Series 8: Personal Diaries, 1878-1884; Vol. 5, 1882, Jan. 1-Feb. 15

original.title: Theodore Roosevelt Papers: Series 8: Personal Diaries, 1878-1884; Vol. 5, 1882, Jan. 1-Feb. 15

text: Most of the members are positively corrupt... singularly inconstant

text: are common thieves . . . they belong to the most dangerous of all classes, the wealthy criminal class. Nevertheless, it is not a question of doing justice to them, it is a question of doing justice to ourselves.
There is a strong and growing feeling of indignation among the people at the actions of these great corporations . . . it is incumbent upon us to see that this feeling takes a lawful shade.
If it becomes evident that these great public robbers cannot be reached by law, then among the people at large the temptation to take action that is outside the law becomes very strong.

For the sake of protecting honest capital, we ought to punish, if we legally can, the deeds of the dishonest wealthy for fear that someday an uprising might come that will overwhelm innocent and guilty alike.
The criminal, is simply a wolf who preys on society and who should be killed or imprisoned like the wolf of the forest.
I represent neither capital nor labor. I represent every American citizen
I can only say that I will try to do them justice.

original.title: Letter to D. H. Clark

text: I hope to see you all home as soon as possible.
James, please put out the light.
see him; he must go to Washington for 10 days; see Senate & House; prevent split on domestic policies.

Home, wife, children, they are what really count in my life. I have heartily enjoyed many things; the Presidency, my success as a soldier, a writer, a big game hunter and explorer; but all of them put together are not for one moment to be weighed in the balence when compared with the joy I have known with your Mother and all of you
